t.2.55.1: When Rāma, devoted to dharma and foremost among those who give delight, had gone to the forest, Kausalyā, weeping and deeply distressed, spoke these words to her husband.
t.2.55.2: Even though your great fame is spread throughout the three worlds, that Rāghava is compassionate, generous, and kind in speech,
t.2.55.3: O best of eminent men, how will those two sons, raised in comfort and now stricken with sorrow, endure hardship in the forest together with Sītā?
t.2.55.5: Having eaten fine food accompanied by excellent sauces and relishes, how will wide-eyed Sītā now partake of the wild fare of nīvāra rice from the forest?
t.2.55.4: She is young, dusky and delicate, accustomed only to comfort. How indeed will Maithilī endure the heat and the cold?
t.2.55.6: Having heard the auspicious sound of song and instrumental music, how will the blameless lady now hear the inauspicious cry of flesh-eating beasts and lions?
t.2.55.7: Where now does he sleep, the mighty-armed one who resembles the great banner of Mahendra, that one of great strength, resting his head upon an arm like an iron bar?
t.2.55.8: When shall I behold the excellent face of Rāma, lotus-hued, framed by beautiful locks of hair, with breath fragrant as the lotus and eyes like lotuses?
t.2.55.9: Surely my heart is made of the very essence of adamant, there is no doubt, since, though I no longer see him, it does not burst into a thousand pieces.
t.2.55.10: If Rāghava returns in the fifteenth year, he would cast aside the kingdom and the treasury, for they will have been enjoyed by Bharata.
t.2.55.11: O lord of the people, once the kingdom has thus been enjoyed by his younger brother, why would the elder and most excellent brother not disdain it?
t.2.55.13: The oblation, the clarified butter, the sacrificial cakes, the kuśa grass and the posts of khadira wood: these, once used and spent, are not employed again in a sacrifice.
t.2.55.12: A tiger does not wish to eat food brought by another; in just the same way, this tiger among men will not care for what has been tasted by another.
t.2.55.14: For Rāma will not be able to accept this kingdom, taken over in this way, any more than wine whose essence has been drawn off, or a sacrifice whose soma has been lost.
t.2.55.15: Rāghava will not endure an insult of this kind, just as a mighty tiger would not endure the touching of its tail.
t.2.55.16: Such as he is, strong as a lion, bull-eyed, a bull among men, he has been struck down by his father himself, as offspring are destroyed by a fish.
t.2.55.17: How can the eternal dharma, practiced by the twice-born and seen in the scriptures, still be yours, if your son, who is devoted to dharma, has been banished by you?
t.2.55.18: A woman's first refuge is her husband, her second refuge is her son, and her third is her kinsmen, O king; a fourth is not found here.
t.2.55.19: Of these, you are not mine, and Rāma has taken refuge in the forest. Nor do I wish to go to the forest, for in every way I have been struck down by you.
t.2.55.21: Hearing these words, laden with harsh sounds, the king too, stricken with sorrow, fell into a swoon. Then the lord of the earth was overwhelmed by grief, and once more he remembered his own evil deed.
t.2.55.20: By you this kingdom, together with its realm, has been destroyed, and likewise your own self along with your ministers; I am destroyed together with my son, and the citizens are destroyed, while your son and your wife are delighted.
